propositions.text: Amirpurya Chavoshy is an Iranian citizen seeking judicial review of a visa officer's refusal of his TRV application.
propositions.quote: Amirpurya Chavoshy is a citizen of Iran. He seeks judicial review of a decision by a visa officer [Officer] to refuse his application for a temporary resident visa [TRV].

propositions.text: The Officer was not satisfied that Dr. Chavoshy would leave Canada after his authorized stay, per s 179(b) IRPR.
propositions.quote: The Officer was not satisfied that Dr. Chavoshy would leave Canada at the end of his authorized stay, as required by s 179(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that Dr. Chavoshy, an Iranian citizen, seeks judicial review of a visa officer's refusal of his TRV application due to concerns about his departure.

propositions.text: The Officer's decision was unreasonable and the judicial review application is allowed.
propositions.quote: For the reasons that follow, the Officer’s decision was unreasonable. The application for judicial review is allowed.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Officer's decision was unreasonable and allows the judicial review application.

propositions.text: Dr. Chavoshy applied for a TRV on June 6, 2024, intending to visit a friend in Vancouver for two weeks starting August 15, 2024.
propositions.quote: Dr. Chavoshy applied for a TRV on June 6, 2024. He stated in his application that he wished to enter Canada on August 15, 2024 for two weeks in order to visit his friend Pejman Najmi, a Canadian permanent resident living in Vancouver.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Dr. Chavoshy applied for a TRV to visit a friend in Vancouver for two weeks starting August 15, 2024.

propositions.text: The application included an invitation letter from Mr. Najmi, who would cover expenses and provided proof of residence and finances.
propositions.quote: Dr. Chavoshy’s application included a letter of invitation from Mr. Najmi, who said he would be responsible for Dr. Chavoshy’s expenses during his visit. Mr. Najmi’s letter attached copies of his permanent residence card, recent bank statements, and proof of property ownership.

propositions.text: Mr. Najmi's bank statements showed a balance of $73,544.
propositions.quote: The bank statements indicated a balance of $73,544.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the application included an invitation letter from Mr. Najmi with proof of residence and finances showing $73,544.

propositions.text: Dr. Chavoshy provided his own bank statements showing $34,002 and proof of property ownership.
propositions.quote: Dr. Chavoshy’s application also included copies of his recent bank statements and documentation confirming property ownership. The bank statements indicated a balance of $34,002.

propositions.text: He also provided prepaid return tickets, medical insurance, and an employer letter confirming leave for the trip.
propositions.quote: Copies of prepaid return tickets and proof of medical insurance were also provided, together with a letter from Dr. Chavoshy’s employer confirming that he had been granted a leave of absence for the trip.

propositions.text: An affidavit confirmed his immediate family all live in Iran.
propositions.quote: The application was supported by an affidavit sworn by Dr. Chavoshy confirming that his mother, father, sister and brother all live in Iran.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Dr. Chavoshy submitted financial documents, return tickets, insurance, employer leave letter, and affidavit of family in Iran.

propositions.text: The Officer reviewed the application and considered several factors in refusing the TRV.
propositions.quote: I have reviewed the application. I have considered the following factors in my decision.

propositions.text: The applicant lacks significant family ties outside Canada.
propositions.quote: The applicant does not have significant family ties outside Canada.

propositions.text: The purpose of the visit is inconsistent with a temporary stay and appears vague and poorly documented.
propositions.quote: The purpose of the applicant’s visit to Canada is not consistent with a temporary stay given the details provided in the application. The applicant’s purpose of visit appears vague and poorly documented.

propositions.text: Information on the host is insufficient.
propositions.quote: Information on host is insufficient.

propositions.text: The Officer is not satisfied the applicant will leave Canada after the authorized stay and refused the application.
propositions.quote: Weighing the factors in this application, I am not satisfied that the applicant will depart Canada at the end of the period authorized for their stay. For the reasons above, I have refused this application.

paragraphs.summary: The Officer found insufficient family ties, vague visit purpose, insufficient host info, and refused the application for lack of departure assurance.

propositions.text: The sole issue is whether the Officer's decision was reasonable.
propositions.quote: The sole issue raised by this application for judicial review is whether the Officer’s decision was reasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court identifies the sole issue as the reasonableness of the Officer's decision.

propositions.text: The Officer's decision is reviewed on a reasonableness standard per Vavilov 2019 SCC 65.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s decision is subject to review by this Court against the standard of reasonableness (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 [Vavilov] at para 10).

propositions.text: Court intervenes only if decision lacks justification, intelligibility, and transparency (Vavilov para 100).
propositions.quote: The Court will intervene only where “there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency” (Vavilov at para 100).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the reasonableness standard from Vavilov and when intervention is warranted.

propositions.text: Justification, intelligibility, and transparency require reasons that explain and support the decision within acceptable outcomes.
propositions.quote: The criteria of “justification, intelligibility and transparency” are met if the reasons allow the Court to understand why the decision was made, and determine whether the decision falls within the range of acceptable outcomes defensible in respect of the facts and law (Vavilov at paras 85-86, citing Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 47).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the criteria for justification, intelligibility, and transparency under Vavilov and Dunsmuir.

propositions.text: The Officer refused the TRV for three reasons: vague visit purpose, insufficient host info, and lack of significant family ties outside Canada.
propositions.quote: The Officer refused Dr. Chavoshy’s application for a TRV for three reasons: (1) the purpose of the visit was vague and poorly documented; (2) the information regarding Dr. Chavoshy’s host was insufficient; and (3) Dr. Chavoshy did not have significant family ties outside Canada.

propositions.text: Dr. Chavoshy disputes all three findings of the Officer.
propositions.quote: Dr. Chavoshy takes issue with all three of these findings.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Officer's three reasons for refusal and that Dr. Chavoshy disputes them all.

propositions.text: Foreign nationals need not provide a complete itinerary or compelling reason to visit Canada.
propositions.quote: The foreign national is not required to provide a complete itinerary of the expected trip. He or she is not required to show a “compelling reason” to visit Canada either (Agidi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 691 at para 7; Singh v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 1210 at para 15).

propositions.text: Abstract, vague, or unsupported reasons may lead to refusal for failure to show intent to leave Canada.
propositions.quote: However, reasons that are abstract, vague or not founded on objective evidence may constitute a factor, among others, that will lead the officer to conclude that the foreign national has not met the burden of demonstrating that he or she will leave Canada at the end of the authorized period of stay (Hamad v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2017 FC 600 at paras 13-16; Omijie v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 878 at para 16).

paragraphs.summary: The court cites precedent that no complete itinerary or compelling reason is required, but vague reasons may justify refusal.

propositions.text: Dr. Chavoshy's application exceeded Kheradpazhooh requirements with a clear, unambiguous purpose and complete itinerary.
propositions.quote: Dr. Chavoshy’s application exceeded the requirements identified by Justice Martineau in Kheradpazhooh. He provided a complete itinerary for the expected trip. While he was not obliged to identify a “compelling reason” for the visit, he explained the nature of his relationship with Mr. Najmi and the difficulties they had encountered in arranging visits in the past. Most importantly, the purpose of the visit was clear and unambiguous. It could not reasonably be described as vague or poorly documented.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Dr. Chavoshy's application met and exceeded requirements with a clear, well-documented visit purpose.

propositions.text: Mr. Najmi's invitation letter explained their friendship and immigration status with supporting financial and property documents.
propositions.quote: Mr. Najmi provided a letter of invitation that explained the history of his friendship with Dr. Chavoshy and his immigration status in Canada. He appended bank statements and proof of property ownership and employment.

propositions.text: It is unclear what further host information could reasonably be provided for a TRV application.
propositions.quote: It is unclear what further information he could have provided respecting his personal circumstances, particularly in the context of an application for a TRV.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Mr. Najmi's invitation and documents sufficient and unclear what more could be provided.

propositions.text: The Officer's claim of no significant family ties outside Canada lacked analysis and contradicted evidence.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s bald statement that Dr. Chavoshy did not have significant family ties outside Canada was unsupported by any analysis and was inconsistent with the evidence provided.

propositions.text: Dr. Chavoshy is unmarried with no children; his parents and siblings live in Iran; he has no family in Canada.
propositions.quote: Dr. Chavoshy is unmarried and does not have children, but his parents and siblings all reside in Iran. He has no family ties in Canada.

propositions.text: He has a long employment history, property ownership in Iran, frequent international travel, and studies in Cyprus as a UNESCO representative.
propositions.quote: His application demonstrated a lengthy history of employment in Iran, property ownership in Iran, and frequent travels to European and other destinations. At the time of his application for a TRV, Dr. Chavoshy was pursuing post-graduate studies in Cypress, where he serves as a UNESCO representative for the coordination of disaster relief efforts.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's family ties finding unsupported and inconsistent with evidence of family, employment, property, travel, and studies.

propositions.text: Visa officers need not provide extensive reasons and have wide discretion entitled to deference.
propositions.quote: Visa officers are not expected to provide extensive reasons for their decisions (Nimely v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2020 FC 282 at para 7). Moreover, visa officers have a wide discretion in assessing the evidence and their decisions are entitled to considerable deference (Chhetri v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2011 FC 872 at para 9).

propositions.text: Visa officers owe a low duty of fairness but must provide reasons understandable to reviewing courts.
propositions.quote: The duty of fairness owed by a visa officer is at the lower end of the spectrum (Nauman v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 964 at para 15). Nevertheless, the reasons must still permit a reviewing court to understand why the decision was made.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites precedent that visa officers have wide discretion, low fairness duty, but must provide understandable reasons.

propositions.text: Visa officers must respond to the factual matrix; reasonableness requires responsiveness, not voluminous reasons.
propositions.quote: Again, while the reality of visa offices and the context in which its officers work include significant operational pressures and resource constraints created by huge volumes of applications, this cannot exempt their decisions from being responsive to the factual matrix put before them. Failing to ask for basic responsiveness to the evidence would deprive reasonableness review of the robust quality that Vavilov requires at paras 13, 67 and 72. “Reasonableness” is not synonymous with “voluminous reasons”: simple, concise justification will do.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites precedent that visa officers must respond to evidence; reasonableness requires responsiveness, not lengthy reasons.

propositions.text: The Officer's reasons lacked justification, intelligibility, and transparency and were therefore unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The Officer’s reasons did not exhibit the requisite degree of “justification, intelligibility and transparency” (Vavilov at paras 85-86). The Officer’s decision was therefore unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Officer's reasons lacked justification, intelligibility, and transparency, making the decision unreasonable.

propositions.text: The judicial review application is allowed and the matter is remitted to a different visa officer for redetermination.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is allowed, and the matter is remitted to a different visa officer for redetermination.

propositions.text: No question was certified for appeal by either party.
propositions.quote: Neither party proposed that a question be certified for appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the judicial review, remits the matter to a different officer, and notes no appeal question was certified.
